title: Distributed Caching Architectures
description: Compare client-side, proxy, and cluster-based distributed caches for large-scale systems.

data.text: Distributed caching spreads cached data across multiple machines so that the cache can grow beyond the memory limits of a single server. This architecture improves scalability, provides high availability through replication, and reduces latency by placing data closer to the services that need it. Designing a distributed cache requires decisions about partitioning, replication, consistency, and failure recovery.

data.title: Distributed Cache Architectures:
items: Client-side caching: Browsers or mobile apps cache responses locally, reducing server requests entirely for repeat views.
Proxy caching: A shared caching proxy such as Varnish sits between clients and servers, caching responses for many clients without application changes.
Cluster caching: A dedicated cache cluster such as Redis Cluster or Memcached pools stores data across multiple nodes, providing horizontal scale and resilience.

data.text: Distributed caches use partitioning to distribute data across nodes and replication to protect against node failures. Consistent hashing is a popular partitioning technique that minimizes data movement when nodes are added or removed. Replication keeps copies of data on multiple nodes so that a single node failure does not cause a cache miss storm. Together, partitioning and replication define the capacity, fault tolerance, and request distribution of the cache cluster.

data.title: Scaling Tip
data.text: Over-provision replication during traffic spikes. If one node fails, replicas absorb the load while the cluster rebalances without degrading user-facing latency.

Distributed caches must detect failed nodes, promote replicas, and rebalance shards automatically. Health checks and gossip protocols help the cluster converge on a consistent view of membership. During recovery, some keys may be temporarily unavailable or served from slightly stale replicas. Understanding the recovery behavior of your cache is essential for designing graceful degradation into the application layer.

rows: Hashing balances load; ranges simplify range queries
Gossip is decentralized but slower to converge
Automatic is faster but risks split-brain

data.text: When to Use a Distributed Cache

Use a distributed cache when a single node cannot hold the working set or when availability requirements demand replication. Session stores, leaderboards, feature flags, and recommendation engines are common candidates. If your working set fits comfortably in a single Redis instance with replication, start simple and scale to a cluster only when monitoring shows memory pressure or throughput saturation.

data.title: Architecture Design Exercise
data.description: You are designing a distributed cache for a social platform with 50 million users and a hot feed that must respond within 20 milliseconds.
steps: Decide whether to use client-side, proxy, or cluster caching for the feed.
Propose a replication factor and failure recovery approach.
data.expectedOutcome: A distributed caching architecture that meets latency, scale, and availability goals.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Distributed caches scale beyond single-node memory limits
Partitioning distributes data; replication provides resilience
Consistency and failure recovery must be designed explicitly
Start simple and evolve to a cluster only when necessary
data.takeaway: A well-designed distributed cache combines sensible partitioning, adequate replication, and clear recovery behavior with the actual scale requirements of the system.
